utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We sit today to hear the final submissions of the Defence in this trial. Good morning, Mr. Djordjevic. Is it intended that the accused have anything directly to say to the Chamber or will you be making submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have agreed that I shall be making the submissions, but if the need arises then the accused will address the Court too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, colleagues of the Prosecution, good morning to everybody. Since the Trial Chamber has already had an opportunity of studying the final brief presented by the Defence, we're not going to deal again with its overall contents. That is why we're going to use this opportunity of pointing to the erroneous understanding and interpretations in the final brief of the Prosecution and also to point out that viewed as a whole the Prosecution has not proved its case or its charges against Mr. Djordjevic and that the Trial Chamber, therefore, should bring in a judgement of acquittal. Over the past three years in the pre-trial phase and the trial phase, the Prosecution and the Defence managed to reach an accord on various agreed facts. In addition to certain facts about which the parties in the proceedings agreed in the pre-trial phase, they also managed to reach an agreement on 263 exhibits before the trial even started. After that, the two parties in these proceedings on several occasions managed to reach an agreement on the acceptability of certain evidence. However, differences remained in an assessment and interpretation of the evidence. The Defence claims that the Prosecution helped pick up its case to try to adapt it to the picture it tried to paint and the story it wished to tell in which Vlastimir Djordjevic is guilty of certain acts which he neither committed nor did he know about them nor did he intend any such acts to be committed. Nor did those acts come under his responsibility as assistant minister of the interior. The Defence is very surprised by the fact and with regret notes that many parts of the Prosecution final brief do not reflect the evidence that was presented during these proceedings, and the conclusions that the Prosecution makes on those grounds are absolutely unfounded and not based on the evidence presented before this Court. Not only did the Prosecution make the wrong conclusions, but in reading the final brief we ascertained that the evidence listed in the footnotes do not reflect the evidence that the Prosecution wishes to prove and that many quotations were tendentious and erroneous and that quotation marks were put to certain facts which the witness never said, and this can be easily verified by looking at the transcript. When somebody quotes something and when quotation marks are put to a passage, it is assumed that he is quoting word for word something that an individual said during his testimony or statement. Unfortunately, in many places of the Prosecution's final brief that has not been the case. Furthermore, instead of providing the witness answers, the Prosecutor is, in fact, quoting his own questions and thereby giving the answers he wished to hear, not what the witness said. What was stated in the paragraphs does not reflect what was stated in the footnotes. Sometimes that is a half truth or something construed by the Prosecution. Sometimes it is completely untrue. The Defence believes in the Trial Chamber, and it also believes that the Prosecutor will not manage to lead the Trial Chamber astray. In view of the limited time that the Defence has for presenting its oral arguments, we will not have occasion to analyse each and every paragraph and the erroneously interpreted piece one by one or footnote or quotation, but we shall only quote a few typical examples. Because of the aforementioned, I should like to ask you that when you come to analyse the final brief of the Prosecution, you pay attention to every quotation and each and every footnote that he uses to support it or where there is lack of support. And therefore, the Trial Chamber should bear in mind three essential points. First, the SRY was a sovereign state which was made up of Serbia and Montenegro. Serbia within its composition had two autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo Metohija. This is of vital importance for understanding the actions taken by the SRJ and Republic of Serbia in all its aspects and understanding the way the MUP functioned with respect to the entire state. In that sense, the other point that you should bear in mind is the following, the time-period during which the events took place. The Prosecution, to a large extent, relied on events from 1998, although in the -- if we look at the indictment, it is evident that the relevant period comprises the time from the 24th of March, 1999, up to the 20th of June, 1999. Your Honours, when you come to analyse the evidence and make your judgement, I'm sure you'll be convinced that Vlastimir Djordjevic in no way is responsible for deportation, forcible transfer, killings, or persecution as stated in the charges in the indictment. The third point that you should bear in mind is the following: All the anti-terrorist actions were undertaken in order to suppress terrorist threats and to neutralise armed combat groups and not against the civilian population. From the evidence you will see that no order, plan, or activity was ever issued, or rather, acted with criminal intent, but in the sense of fighting against burgeoning terrorism in the province of Kosovo and Metohija. As is now the Prosecutor wishes to prove joint criminal enterprise and you need a criminal element in order to prove that. What is necessary is that a joint plan for a joint criminal enterprise includes the committing of a crime under statute para 1036, the state of SRY fought against strong terrorist forces who, according to certain assessments, under military control held up to 75 per cent of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. They terrorised the civilian population and represented a threat to legitimate state organs. The fact that terrorism had its stronghold in the secessionist intentions cannot make it acceptable. The international community did nothing to help the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in its struggle against terrorism. Already at the beginning the SRY was thought to be the bad guy and the international community portrayed it as such and tried to tie the state's hands in its struggle against terrorism on its sovereign territory, allowing terrorist forces to increase and to manipulate the situation in a way which led to the terrible events which happened in the course of 1999. Entering into an analysis of the allegations in this trial, the Prosecution endeavoured to include a highly superficial political history and the history of events which represented a framework for the events that took place in the course of 1998 and 1999. The Prosecution completely erroneously portrays relevant history and does not base it on objective sources but exclusively on the assertions made by Albanian politicians and journalists. With respect to historical issues, the Prosecution first of all quotes Fred Abrahams from the Organisation of Human Rights Watch. Here it is necessary to state that Mr. Abrahams is not an expert nor did the Prosecution call him as an expert in historical matters. The Prosecution as we see quotes Mr. Abrahams as an objective source; however, he did not have at his disposal facts which would enable him to view the situation in a neutral way. Without a doubt he confirmed that he didn't even read the constitutional texts and laws which represent the basis for understanding key historical events. In addition to that, as we stressed in our final brief, Mr. Abrahams stated -- well, gave his version of historical events on the 24th of January, 2002, several months after he was -- he interviewed Ibrahim Rugova, the leader of the Secessionist DLK [as interpreted] Party; the Albanian politician, Veton Surroi; and Albanian journalist, Baton Haxhiu. A historical overview which was presented without conducting interviews with Serbian politicians and journalists and without getting to know the relevant legal texts can be nothing more than a synthesis of an interview which was published on behalf of the Prosecution in co-operation with the investigators of the OTP. Therefore, it is not surprising that the facts which Mr. Abrahams presents as being historical facts coincide with the statements made by these persons. Reading and listening to the arguments presented by the Prosecution, everybody who is an observer might think that the Serbs illegally and unlawfully conducted an invasion against a third independent country. I think that we must all bear in mind that everything that took place took place in Serbia, a state in which its army and its police had every right to be on the territory of its own country. What would have happened in any other country in the world, I ask you, had burgeoning terrorism, rebellions, secessionist, or whatever we like to call it, movement tried by armed struggle to cut off parts of its sovereign territory? Every country would respond to that in similar fashion, as did the SRJ and Serbia to save its country and retain its territorial integrity and sovereignty. Whether the emotions of a nation, the emotions it has towards its country and its territory is something unusual, no it is normal that every country in every state of the world has patriotic feelings in the country in which he lives, where he was born, where his forefathers lived, where his sons live, and to which he belongs. The initial thesis of the Prosecution – that the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise was to ensure lasting Serb control over the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija which is an integral part of Serbia – is completely absurd. I assume that each country has the right to have control over its integral part. What would the world look like if in every country some group, regardless of how numerous it is, through armed force, wished to cut off a part of its territory and the state organs have -- do not have the right to react to those acts of violence? As the beginnings of the plan to retain lasting Serbian control over the province in paragraph 37, which is to be found in the portion describing the legal changes by which the Serb leadership wanted to place Kosovo under its direct control, mention is made of special measures taken by the Presidency of the SFRY. The SFRY is not Serbia; it is a Federation within which Serbia, with its two autonomous provinces, was just one of the member states. The Prosecution forgets or intentionally leaves out the fact that those measures were introduced because of the violence of Kosovo Albanians and that Serbia did not introduce it, but a federal state which was then made up of Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and finally Serbia. Those measures were taken by the Presidency of the SFRY within the frameworks of its constitutional authority and it was supported by the Assembly of the SFRY because they were undertaken in order to safe-guard the territorial integrity and constitutional order of the SFRY, securing public law and order, freedom, life, work, and the normalisation of the overall situation in the autonomous province of Kosovo. The Prosecution furthermore states in paragraphs 50 and 51 that the Assembly of the SFRY adopted a programme of preventing the emigration of Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo in January 1990, which condemns the implementation of the goals of Albanian nationalists for an ethnically pure Kosovo. And this quotes an example that the Serbian political leadership was convinced that the demographic balance of Kosovo had to be changed in order to retain political control over the province. We should once again like to stress that this programme was adopted by the Assembly of the SFRY, that is to say six member states, not the Serb leadership. Would the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia and its declaration adopted on the 27th of November, 1992, on human rights and the rights of national minorities, would it observe in point 4 of the declaration - and this is otherwise Exhibit P55 - what it did observe with -- by providing exact information and which is only in part stressed by the Prosecution in paragraph 52 of its final brief that none of this happened. And finally, in paragraph 53 the Prosecution states and draws the conclusion that this inflammatory rhetoric led to systematic crimes against the Kosovo Albanians stipulated in the indictment. This kind of conclusion is only one completely distorted political construction which the Prosecution wished to present in order to justify its accusations. No difference is made between the decisions taken by the former SFRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and Serbia, and they don't enter into the reasons for which all these states had to undertake certain measures on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. In 1999, the Republic of Serbia was a component part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as one of its member, the other was the Republic of Montenegro. Kosovo and Metohija as well as the autonomous province of Vojvodina were integral parts of the Republic of Serbia. Within the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, you had Albanians, Montenegrins, Serbs, Turks, and Roma, as well as other minorities living there. And regardless of their national affiliation, they had equal political and other rights just like everybody else in Serbia, all other Serbian citizens. Since the constitution of the Republic of Serbia passed on the 28th of September, 1990, determined the sovereignty of the Republic of Serbia and that the republic belonged to all its citizens. In the Republic of Serbia, the autonomous province of Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija forms a territorial autonomy. In official use in the Republic of Serbia, you had the Serbo-Croatian language, and in the areas of the Republic of Serbia where nationalities lived, they were able to use their language and script in the manner prescribed by law. The separatist aspirations of the Albanians have their roots in the mid-1960s of the 20th sentry when the slogan was put forward "Kosovo Republic." And just as Witness Jokanovic in these proceedings explained to us, this slogan represented the call of the Albanian separatists for Kosovo and Metohija from a non-state status to be given the status of a republic, which meant the status of a state, and thereby members of the Federation and the right to self-determination until secession. In the history of Yugoslav federalism Kosovo and Metohija never had the status of a state, just like the autonomous province of Vojvodina, with the proviso that the position of the autonomous provinces changed depending on the will of the ruling political majority which was manifest through the constitutions of the SFRY and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The secessionist demands of the Albanian political parties did not have as their aim to realise the rights of the Albanian nation within the frameworks of the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslavia, in view of the fact that those rights were equal rights enjoyed by all, but the secession from Serbia and Yugoslavia and the founding of an independent and autonomous state of Kosovo. With the establishment and actions of the KLA, an armed struggle was proclaimed as the sole means of accomplishing the political goal of creating an independent state of Kosovo and secession from the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecutor's interpretation of the political historical context is mostly incorrect. Every sovereign country in the world is authorised and takes measures to preserve its territorial integrity and sovereignty. You cannot have in one state, in addition to legal organs of authority, a parallel system of power and authority in existence because a political group rallied on a national basis which is to secede and conducts illegal elections for these alleged organs and forms their own police and army. Acts of this kind in all countries are termed anti-constitutional and are punishable. When such subversive actions take on concrete forms in the formation of a parallel MUP or Ministry of Defence and start anti-constitutional acts, then criminal prosecution is a legitimate response of any state to such phenomena and events. Would a single country in the world tolerate to have in its state schools, universities, faculties, tuition according to tuitions powers and programmes of some other state, I ask you? Isn't it normal that in one country a teaching plan and programme is applied of the country on which territory it is and throughout its territory. In mid-1998, along with the material and financial assistance from abroad, the KLA undertook broad-based terrorist activities to cut off Kosovo and Metohija from Serbia. Because of attacks against members of the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia, kidnapping of civilians and killing of civilians, non-Albanians and Albanians alike, who did not want to join the terrorist forces, cutting across the main communication routes and preventing normal activity from taking place and taking territory by the KLA, the state was forced to defend the sovereigty and territorial integrity, lives and property of all citizens living on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Bearing in mind all of the above, OTP's thesis and conclusions about origins of the JCE are erroneous and especially with regard to the place and role of Vlastimir Djordjevic. Vlastimir Djordjevic is charged with being a member of the JCE, together with Slobodan Milosevic, Nikola Sainovic, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, Sreten Lukic, Dragoljub Ojdanic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Vladimir Lazarevic, as well as Radomir Markovic, Obrad Stevanovic, and Dragan Ilic. Vlastimir Djordjevic was a professional member of the MUP and he acted in keeping with the laws and regulations of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as well as decisions by competent state bodies and he did not participate in the creation of the state policies. He undertook measures and actions within the remit of his position in the republican MUP in keeping with Minister Stojiljkovic's decisions. He never attended any meeting where political issues were discussed or where political decisions were made. He was not a member of any political party including even the ruling SPS. He attended meetings upon invitation by President Milan Milutinovic and the minister of the interior Vlajko Stojiljkovic as part of MUP delegations, and at such meetings the security of the state was discussed. He never got involved in any discussions at the meetings that he attended. He didn't report or contributed to any decision-making processes. Vlastimir Djordjevic did not have any personal relationship with Slobodan Milosevic, and his only contact with him were at official meetings. Djordjevic did not receive a single task from Milosevic and he did not act pursuant to his orders or tasks and no single evidence to that fact was adduced. In para 18, the OTP alleges that Milosevic had very significant de facto authorities over the MUP without any corroboration. His allegations that Milosevic implemented control over the Joint Command through Sainovic and Minic, the OTP in paragraph 262, footnote 586, proves, based on the testimony of Witness Vasiljevic. In 1998 Witness Vasiljevic was already retired and he didn't attend a single Joint Command meeting in the course of 1998. There is no single record establishing that either he or Minic attended either of the meetings in 1999, especially not a meeting with Vasiljevic. Witness Vasiljevic pointed out that he presented his view of Sainovic's authority over Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic, and he never even mentioned Djordjevic. In transcript that's page 5699 to page number 5700. He met the president of the Republic of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, only at meetings as part of the delegations of the Republic of Serbia MUP headed by the minister. Vlastimir Djordjevic met Nikola Sainovic at meetings within the framework of the MUP delegations, and in 1998 during the implementation of the plan for countering terrorism, he participated at meetings in Pristina attended by politicians, soldiers, and policemen. However, he did not receive a single order from Sainovic and there is no evidence to corroborate that. There is no single piece of evidence that Sainovic issued a single task to Djordjevic, that he was his superior, and that Djordjevic reported to Sainovic. One has to bear in mind that Sainovic was the vice-president of the federal government, and as of October 1998 he was also the president of the commission for cooperation with the KVM. And that he had contacts with the MUP and the staff of the MUP in Pristina within the framework of his authorities and tasks. In the course of 1999 during the war, the only meeting that Sainovic took place in the month of May when a report was submitted to the Supreme Command Staff. Djordjevic had a single meeting with General Ojdanic in May 1999 at the debriefing to the superior command staff. All the other contacts with -- at the Supreme Command Staff and the Main Staff of the army were by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. During 1998 and during 1999, General Ojdanic, pursuant to the decision of this Tribunal, IT-05-87, dated 26 February 2009, was not marked as a member of the JCE and the OTP did not appeal that part of the decision. Djordjevic met Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic during the war on 18 April 1999, in Pristina, where he stayed for one day when Lukic was invited to the PRK, and when Lukic and Stevanovic learned about the order of the resubordination of the MUP to the chief of the Main Staff, General Ojdanic. On the -- as well as on 6 the 4th of May, 1999, when he attended a debriefing at the Supreme Command Staff. General Lazarevic, according to the decision of this Tribunal, IT-05-87, dated 26th February 2009, was not marked as a member of the JCE, and the Prosecution did not appeal that part of the decision. Vlajko Stojiljkovic was the minister of the interior and Vlastimir Djordjevic's superior. In keeping with the decisions of Minister Stojiljkovic, in 1999 Djordjevic did not spend any time in Kosovo and Metohija. He was rather in Belgrade, where he was in charge of the RJB in all of its activities, save for the anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija, as that part of the work was entrusted to the MUP staff for the countering terrorism pursuant to the minister's decision. And unlike in 1998, his presence in Kosovo in 1999 was either to escort the minister or on his order, due to activities that were not related to suppression of terrorism. Stojiljkovic was responsible for the work of the MUP in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, and in keeping with his authorities he could alter the regular organisation and the authorities of the MUP, which indeed he did when he issued a decision on the establishing of the MUP staff, dated 16 June 1998, and when he transferred the RJB authorities and responsibilities of the RJB chief to the MUP staff, which he had established. He also transferred some of the authorities of the RDB and the responsibilities of the RDB chief. Therefore, when it comes to implementing tasks pertaining to the competence of the MUP staff, the head of the staff for countering terrorism is responsible exclusively to the minister and nobody else. Radomir Markovic, up to the end of November 1998, was the assistant minister of the interior in charge of the crime police and analysis, and then pursuant to a decision by the minister, he was assigned to the position as the chief of the RDB and stayed in that position throughout the war. Markovic, as an assistant minister and as the chief of the RDB, received his tasks exclusively from the minister. The minister was his only superior and the department chiefs could not issue tasks to each other. Pursuant to the ministerial decision on the establishing of the staff for countering terrorism, the task for countering terrorism, a special security task in Kosovo and Metohija were transferred to the MUP staff which comprised members of both the departments and their organisational units in Kosovo and Metohija as well as the police units deployed there. The police chiefs of neither of the departments could issue tasks for the MUP staff for countering terrorism, nor could they issue tasks to the members of their units belonging to their departments who were sent to Kosovo and Metohija for anti- -- to counter anti-terrorist activities and to engage in special security tasks. In the course of 1999 Radomir Markovic and Vlastimir Djordjevic discharged duties as the chiefs of departments within the remits defined by the minister. General Obrad Stevanovic was the assistant minister in charge of the line of work of the police administration and the operative centre of the high school and the police academy. The Prosecutor's allegation that Obrad Stevanovic was the chief of the police administration were not proven, and his function and position cannot be proven by anybody's statement. And the reference in the Prosecutor's final brief, which allegedly proves that Stevanovic was the chief of the police administration in 1999, is contrary to the statement by Witness Cvetic, para 21 of the OTP's final brief, footnote 27, and in several other places we can find the same thing. If -- one can see that Stevanovic was the assistant minister in the decision on the establishment of the ministerial collegium, dated 4 December 1998, Exhibit D208, and primarily from the dispatch, dated 4th of June, 1997, Exhibit P263 where the lines of work of the assistant minister are defined. In all minutes of the MUP Staff where General Obrad Stevanovic was present, he is always mentioned as the assistant minister and not a single time as the chief of the administration of the police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down for the benefit of one and all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major-General Sreten Lukic, pursuant to the minister -- the decision of the minister of the interior, dated 16 June 1998, was appointed chief of the staff of the MUP for countering terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. Pursuant to a decision, Exhibit P57, the tasks that were given to the Staff derogated the competencies of both MUP departments to the extent that their competencies and responsibilities had been transferred to the MUP Staff, therefore Sreten Lukic could not be answerable to Vlastimir Djordjevic for his work or be subordinated to him or to the RDB chief, but only to the minister who had taken that decision. By its nature, the staff was an inter-departmental body. It comprised both the RJB and the RDB as well -- in terms of both the personnel and the organisation and that's why it was answerable only to the minister. The minister entrusted the planning, organisation, and the management of anti-terrorist activities and special security tasks to the MUP staff. Therefore, the head of the staff could be answerable to -- for his work and the work of the Staff only to the minister and the minister was the only person who could give him any tasks or orders. General Dragan Ilic was the chief of the crime police administration. From the 4th of December, 1998, he was appointed a member of the collegium. The only chief of the RJB administration from the base of the minister who was appointed a member of the collegium by name was the chief of the UKP and all the other chiefs of the RJB administration attended the collegium meetings upon minister's invitations. I would like to point to an error in the transcript, line 21 on page 16, one word is missing, and that is the MUP staff. When minister general -- when General Radomir Markovic was assigned to the position of the chief of the RDB, pursuant to a decision on the minister, the minister did not appoint the assistant minister in charge of the work of the crime police, and when he appointed him as a collegium member, the minister directly issued tasks to the chief of the UKP, General Ilic, both at collegium meetings as well as during their personal contacts. There's no single piece of evidence that General Dragan Ilic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise. The OTP persistently insinuates that there was indeed a plan but that plan simply did not exist. In its final brief, the OTP continuously mentions the names of certain persons who were allegedly members of the joint criminal enterprise, despite the fact that those persons were tried, and at their trials it was not established that they were members of any joint criminal enterprise. All the elements which point to the existence of guilt have to be proven beyond any reasonable doubt. The audacious allegations are simply not enough to deprive a person of his freedom. In no event did the OTP prove beyond any reasonable doubt how could Vlastimir Djordjevic fit into the allegations contained in the indictment, let alone how he can be held responsible for any of those allegations. Vlastimir Djordjevic is sitting in this courtroom today only because he was the chief of the RJB and the assistant minister during the relevant time-period. There is no evidence about his criminal intent or actions. The Trial Chamber cannot hold him responsible only because of the fact that during the relevant period he was in a certain position in the Ministry of the Interior. At that time, a large number of people worked in the MUP and they had all sorts of different authorities. There were other assistant ministers, but those people are not here today. They are not accused before this Tribunal. And when I say that, I mean Obrad Stevanovic, Rade Markovic, Dragan Ilic, and let's stop there. The Prosecution alleges that those men were also members of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution put those men on their witness list, but it did not bring them in to provide testimony before this Trial Chamber. One thing is certain: If there were -- if there was any information about the existence of any plan, this -- these people would have that information. So how come they were not invited, they were not called to testify? They were not called to testify only because of the fact that they do not have the information about the existence of any such plan. They were not called to testify because they did not have any information that would charge Vlastimir Djordjevic. Therefore, people who closely co-operated with Djordjevic were not brought here to testify because they do not have any information that would corroborate the Prosecutor's allegations and there is no such information in the -- in the record. The OTP alleges that there was a joint criminal enterprise aimed at committing crimes alleged in the indictment. According to the Prosecutor's allegations contained in the second paragraph, the goal of that alleged joint criminal enterprise was to secure permanent Serbian control over the autonomous province of Kosovo by way of changing the ethnic balance. That goal, which is to secure permanent control over one's own territory in its own, is not a criminal goal. During the relevant period, Kosovo and Metohija was part of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and therefore it was only justified for that territory to be under the control of Serbia. The problem actually was the fact that that control was being permanently lost under the wave of terrorism and criminal -- crime. All efforts undertaken to regain control were aimed against or targeted against the terrorist army, which according to all the descriptions represented a strong force and which did not adhere either to the rules of warfare or the rules of the cease-fire agreed with the mediation of the international community. In order to prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, one has to prove the existence of the following criminal element, and that is that at the joint plan of that joint criminal enterprise included the commission of a crime envisaged by the statute, paragraph 1036. In that sense, the Prosecution did not prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise; on the contrary. The state organs were duty-bound to provide for the security of their own citizens. More specifically, the Ministry of the Interior was duty-bound to secure the security of its own citizens which included their protection from terror and violence -- acts of violence committed by terrorist forces, as well as to protect citizens from shelling and other extraordinary circumstances. This duty unambiguously arises from Article 1 of the Law of the Internal Affairs and Article 2 of the rules of the internal organisation of the MUP. All crimes alleged in the indictment are part of the plan which allegedly was implemented in -- during the period between the 24th of March and the 20th of June, 1999. The OTP continuously imposes an allegation that 800.000 Kosovan Albanians were expelled from the province, but they didn't manage to prove why they left. The numbers are unclear in terms of their ethnicity, and the only thing that Mr. Neil Wright could present was the fact that Albanians from Kosovo constituted a large majority. If, according to the estimates, approximately 80 to 85 Kosovar Albanians lived in the territory, why is it strange then that the large majority of the people who left the territory were, in fact, ethnic Albanians? No one has put in any effort to determine how many members of other ethnic communities left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in the relevant period. This information would confirm that the percentage of the people from other ethnic communities that left Kosovo and Metohija was proportionately greater than that of the Albanian population. Since no evidence has been adduced as to the way in which this plan was adopted, what it contained, who was in charge of the plan, and what it was supposed to achieve, the Prosecution is trying to show that this plan must have existed, stating in its paragraph 48 -- 458 the following: [In English] "The scale of the crimes, their repetition in village after village throughout Kosovo and the sheer number of victims demonstrate that there was an organised high-level plan to persecute and expel Kosovo Albanians and discourage them from ever returning." [Interpretation] As the Prosecution claims, a conclusion must be drawn to that effect on the basis of crime-base evidence, despite the lack of any evidence that anyone had actually planned or ordered anything of the sort. Crime-base evidence does not show that the plan even existed, the plan that the Prosecution is trying to show existed. There was movement of population and there were crimes, but one cannot draw a conclusion from that that there must have been a plan. This was merely a result of a situation in a war-ravaged area, a situation in which movement of population was a logical consequence. The Prosecution claims that there must have been a campaign of expulsion; however, it is quite strange that the Prosecution fails to take into account the fact that the rest of the people left too and the percentage was the same, as highlighted in the final brief of the Defence and as presented in the UNHCR data. It is quite astounding that 17.500 mostly Serbs left Kosovo in the period of only three days, between the 14th and the 16th of June; we can see that in Exhibit P737 and at pages 21 to 23. This was certainly a sizeable percentage of the Serb population that still remained in Kosovo and Metohija and it occurred in the time-period relevant for the indictment. Those Serbs left the province of their own free will, in the same way in which the rest of the population had done in the previous months, not in line with any plan. If you have a war in a certain area, then as a consequence the population will flee. Several witnesses in their statements and their evidence before the Court stated that they simply feared the unknown. There is a very small number of examples that indicates that there was the pattern that the Prosecution is trying to depict as a co-ordinated widespread and systematic. There are many more examples of people hearing this kind of rumours and leaving because there was a campaign to spread fear. Some witnesses in their evidence stated that they had been told to leave, but not by Serbs but by KLA members or their village elders. Whatever their motives, they cannot be represented as a plan to expel the Kosovar Albanians. A large number of these people left for Montenegro, which was part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Many left for Serbia proper, north of Kosovo, although the UNHCR did not put in a lot of effort to actually record how many of them and who they were. There is absolutely no reason why those people would want to leave to the areas -- to those areas had they really been fleeing the forces of the FRY or Serbia. Crime-base evidence adduced by the Prosecution does not corroborate the conclusion that there was an organised plan or orchestrated efforts. This evidence confirms quite the opposite. There was a climate of war, chaos, and confusion. The Prosecution is trying to show that there was a plan to expel people, but the evidence adduced before this Court confirms that this was, in fact, voluntary movement of people, of population. This evidence shows that people chose, of their own free will, to leave the areas where there was fierce fighting, where bombs rained down, and where they lacked basic means of livelihood. There is virtually no evidence that would fit into this pattern the Prosecution alleges existed to the fact that the Serb forces methodically channelled Albanian refugees to the borders and transit points. This is at para 512. Quite the opposite. The record abounds with evidence of groups moving from town to town within Kosovo because people thought that they should go wherever the group is going. In several situations the Serb forces actually made those people go back. There is nothing systematic in this kind of movement of people which would amount to evidence of the existence of any kind of methodical plan. Based on the examination of the crime-base evidence, it is quite clear that people left for a variety of reasons, mostly boiling down to their personal choice, to go to safer areas. It was a matter of personal choice then and not a widespread and systematic plan, as alleged in the indictment. All evidence of all the witnesses should be considered very carefully in order to discern the real reason for their departure instead of settling for what the Prosecution is claiming. In many cases, the Prosecution indicated that the witness would testify of about how he or she was expelled and in the course of the cross-examination it would turn out that they had gone because they had heard something was going on or because they hadn't felt safe. For every allegation of deportation or forcible transfer, it is necessary to prove that there was a lack of choice on the part of the alleged victim and the intent to effect the permanent displacement. Mr. President, Your Honour, I would now like us to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to prove that within a joint criminal enterprise there was a plan that covered the commission of those crimes, one has to ask how the plan would be implemented without any orders or instructions. There is no link between the acts committed on the ground attributable to irresponsible individuals and the putative plan made at higher levels simply because there was no any such plan. There's only any attempt on the part of the Prosecution to establish a link between all the tragic incidents that happened during the state of war. In order to corroborate its arguments, the Prosecution is trying to bring back the images of the Holocaust of the Second World War, especially when it alleges that there was organised transport and the destruction of the personal identification documents in order to wipe out those persons' identities. However, these allegations are unfounded and they cannot serve to show there was any kind of a plan. As regards the organised transport, the Prosecution is trying to paint a picture of people being rounded up, being put on board trains and buses and taken away; however, the evidence does not corroborate this vision painted by the Prosecution. The only evidence, as regards the organised transport, pertains to the scheduled departures of trains and buses and just a few buses. At the worst there were just a few special trains and buses added to the regular timetable to accommodate a large number of people who wanted to leave. In order to corroborate its argument that people were transported out of the country, the Prosecution relies on the evidence presented by Bajram Bucaliu. However, Bucaliu, who was familiar with the timetable, actually says that he decided to go to Macedonia on a scheduled train departing at 8.00 a.m. When they were not allowed to cross the border on that day, and this strikingly undermines the argument that there was a plan to deport those people, the people went back home and the next day they simply returned to the railway station to catch the next train. In addition to Bucaliu, the Prosecution relies for the most part on the testimony of Witness Nazalie Bala. What is missing from her description of how she went to the railway station is the fact that the Pristina city centre had been fiercely bombed on the 28th and the 29th of March. It is reasonable to assume that people were panic-stricken when bombs started falling in their midst. The evidence of this witness is consistent with the evidence of Emin Kabashi, in that they both say they saw a large number of people on the railway station. However, Kabashi does not say that people were forced to board the trains. In fact, Kabashi waited there for three days before he was able to leave with his family. Furthermore, unlike Witness Bala, Kabashi does not say anything about being forced to cross the border at Djeneral Jankovic. In fact, he stayed the next six days there waiting. Generally speaking, the claims made by Witness Bala about the armed forces guarding the buses are questionable as regards their reliability, and her political affiliation and interests bring into doubt her credibility, especially in light of the fact that she has ties with the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Liberties and she's a member of the Democratic Party of Kosovo led by Hashim Thaqi, Exhibit P421, transcript page 2176. When there was evidence about the buses in a small number of cases, they were often hired by witnesses themselves because they wanted to leave. This proved to be the case in Gerxhaliu's case who organised transportation by bus to Montenegro, and in Morine's evidence who says that the buses were hired by civilians, Exhibit P284, transcript page 930. The Prosecution also relies on claims made by Halit and Hyseni Berisha as regards to two buses in Suva Reka. That's P598, page 4, and Hyseni is testifying about the same thing. The buses were used to transport people who left the town and did not have their own cars. It is not known who actually hired those two buses. This was not part of any systematic pattern as the Prosecution would like to show. This was just a couple of buses hired by unidentified private persons. These were not elements of a system effecting the expulsion, just privately hired buses used by the people to leave this area until the air-strikes finished and until the state of war ended. This is all the evidence adduced in order to prove there was a comprehensive plan to transport people out of the country. However, the Prosecution simply used the regular transportation system and scheduled departures to depict them as a system for the deportation. This was not sufficient to prove that there was a plan, just as it would not be sufficient to go to central station here in The Hague. Let me illustrate the point in this way where you can see the railway traffic going on. If you had the state of war in the Netherlands now, there would be armed guards in the station and it would be full of people trying to leave and seek shelter in other areas nearby. There's absolutely nothing which would show us how the transportation was organised in order to achieve the deportation of the people because there was no such organisation of the transportation, especially not one that could be called widespread and systematic. The same goes for the allegations regarding the confiscation and destruction of IDs. The Prosecution is trying to show that as a part of a comprehensive, unwritten tacit plan; however, if we analyse the evidence carefully, the Trial Chamber will see that there is virtually not a single case where the witnesses themselves lost their personal IDs. In their evidence they, in most cases, say they heard about that happening or that they thought they saw it happen to other people, and it is quite strange that we are expected to believe that the witnesses who testified before this Tribunal are exceptions who accidentally managed to keep their documents with them. It is absolutely impossible to even try to understand how this could be a part of a widespread and systematic plan when in the record you have evidence that after their IDs were checked people received their IDs, were given back their IDs, as Witness Florim Elmi Krasniqi said at page 631 -- at Exhibit P631, page 6. In paragraph 502 the Prosecution notes that Krasniqi and other witnesses were not left without their personal IDs, which is in full opposition to the existence of a methodical plan. The most compelling evidence on the confiscation of personal documents was provided by Gerxhaliu who said the following: "[In English] Those documents that were issued in Albanian language by the Ministry of the Interior of Kosova, then they tore them up and threw them away." [Interpretation] That's transcript page 3120 -- 29. It is important to mention this, in view of the fact that the Ministry of the Interior of Kosovo did not exist. That personal documentation was issued by the parallel authority which was unlawfully established on the territory of the sovereign republic of Serbia. If certain personal documents were confiscated at all, what happened was what usually happens with unlawfully issued personal documents, which are always of course confiscated. An example of this was provided by Emin Kabashi, who stated that only the IDs of women were checked. The fact that men's ID cards were not checked shows that there was no consistent plan; and secondly, the ID card of one woman was returned, and that's in transcript 2374. The fact that the unlawful parallel government issued personal documents explains stories similar to this, where one ID card was returned while another was confiscated. Only unlawfully issued personal documents were confiscated, and this can be seen from the fact that the witnesses frequently crossed the border with their legal passports and just threw away the Kosovo ID cards. It is important to stress that the documents were very frequently handed over even when not asked for, as we were able to see from the evidence adduced, the keeping back of lawful documents had no negative repercussions. The Prosecutor is trying to make a big thing out of the burning of personal documents on the basis of what was stated by General Drewienkiewicz and Ciaglinski. According to General DZ, he just quickly glanced through six documents which were in a heap of documents that were burnt. He never confirmed what type of documents they were and it wouldn't be unreasonable to expect that those six documents belonged to Kosovo Albanians, while in that heap of other documents you had documents belonging to other ethnicities. He does not know who set fire to the documents nor why they were burnt, so that the observation made that this was part of a plan is mere speculation, especially bearing in mind the fact that General DZ himself was not convinced that any plan ever existed. There are several reasonable reasons which could be ascribed to the burning of documents, and one of those reasons is that they -- it meant the destruction of old or archived documents, documents which had expired. The fact that Ciaglinski saw the burning of a large quantity of archive material immediately before the MUP left the territory reinforces this theory. Ciaglinski saw that various documents were being destroyed, not only ID cards, and that is to be found on transcript page 5377 to 5378. He also has a photograph on which you can't see much except for a bit of smoke, but he has no photographs showing the documents themselves. In addition to that, he did not show us any burnt documents which he says he took. Although he was not able to comment the destruction of the archive as a routine part of the work of every organisation, Michael Phillips testified that the KLM did the same before it withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija. He explained that they did not do that because they wanted to hide that documentation from anyone, but quite simply that they didn't want to leave the documentation behind, so that finally they ended up by destroying large quantities of material, transcript page 8748. There is no reason why we should not apply the same rule to old citizens' archives in Kosovo and Metohija. Witness K54 never received any such orders nor did any member of the Army of Yugoslavia receive them or the MUP, nor did they testify that they'd ever received any orders of that kind. Witness K54 testified that he was at the border crossings but he never saw that personally taking place, transcript page 4389, 4418 to 4419. Generally speaking, in the records there's no proof or evidence that the checking or confiscation of personal documents was widespread and systematic and that it was a policy. Moreover, there is no proof that any such policy ever existed or that any of the border authorities were informed of any such plan. The confiscation of ID cards in order to wipe out somebody's identity would have absolutely no effects since citizens, just like in any other country, were able to get new ID documents at any time. The basic documents of citizens were never destroyed and all citizens of Kosovo and Metohija could have issued their birth certificates and other personal documents. They could do this on the territory of Serbia and also in the consular offices of the SRY abroad. They did that then and they're still doing it today. When it comes to accusations relating to the crime of murder, the Prosecution has failed to show that those acts were ordered, or rather, that there exists any link between the murders and some sort of plan. Even in cases where the Trial Chamber can ascertain that the crime of a murder took place, these were unfortunate incidents involving individuals and they were acts which were in no way linked to any sort of plan or joint criminal enterprise. Adding incidents in Podujevo into the indictment is something which weakened the Prosecution's arguments most, because this incident is absolutely contrary to the existence of any such plan which would be implemented. The incident in Podujevo occurred on the 28th of March, 1999, and it coincides in the -- within the period, which according to theory -- the theory of the Prosecution, the Serb forces were implementing the forcible transfer of individuals, murder, prosecution, according to a plan, including deportation. However, in Podujevo there was no plan for expulsion. If there existed a widespread and systematic plan, why then did not that plan incorporate Podujevo too? Because there was no plan and the Prosecution knows full well that the evidence related to the incident in Podujevo are directly against the grain of the existence of any all-embracing plan. Although in Podujevo an act of murder had taken place, it is clear that it wasn't ordered nor permitted nor accepted, even less so. Assistance to the victims was given by the doctors of MUP. The victims were sent to hospitals in Pristina and Belgrade. Had there really been a widespread and systematic plan, none of these measures would have been taken. The forensic evidence presented by the Prosecution is not convincing enough. With respect to the incident in Izbica, there is great doubt about where the bodies were found first and under what conditions and how these individuals lost their lives in the first place. There are significant indices to show that instead of a crime there was a montage, and the Court should reach the conclusion that the forensic evidence presented was suspect, fraught with doubt, and therefore cannot be used to support the allegations made by the Prosecution. The same is true for Kotlina, where the site of the crime was contaminated by the villagers much before the official investigating teams arrived on the spot, even during the investigation. In addition to that, the Prosecution theory does not coincide with the report of the Austrian forensic team either. In numerous cases the forensic evidence quite simply does not tally with the testimony given by witnesses. As an example Dr. Stankovic testified that the Austrian report on the alleged killings in Kacanik in no way supports the allegations contained in the statement given by Witness Hazbi, Loku. The crime base is not connected with Vlastimir Djordjevic at all and is difficult for the Defence to respond because it is so far-fetched and far away from his responsibilities. Numerous witnesses were called who spoke of the original want -- alleged wanton destruction, but it is considered that the damage was not seen by witnesses. Riedlmayer also couldn't confirm who inflicted the damage, let alone the intention to intentionally commit damage. The Prosecution says that Riedlmayer's findings, as well as what the witnesses saw on the ground, shows that the Serbs intentionally destroyed Albanian cultural and religious sites. There is no evidence which shows that anybody committed these crimes with the intention coinciding with the crime of persecution. Riedlmayer has absolutely no qualifications or expertise on which to base his assessments and evaluations. This area was subject to different combat operations, and therefore collateral damage represents a reasonable explanation for fires and shooting. Certainly without reliable witnesses, we cannot ascribe this to the SRJ forces in Serbia only on the basis of assumptions. The Prosecution claims: [In English] "The targeted nature of the damage demonstrates that it was the result of deliberate acts by the Serb forces, not NATO air-strikes. Religious and cultural sites of Serbs and other ethnicities were spared." [Interpretation] Not only is that not true, but on the basis of this one cannot conclude anything about who and why inflicted damages on those facilities. We must remind ourselves that there were military operations underway and that the protection of cultural heritage does not represent a priority if such facilities are being used for military purposes. And there we have a related judgement of the Blaskic trial judgement, paragraph 185, see also the Second Protocol of The Hague Convention of 1954, Article 6. Certain evidence indicates that the damage inflicted was caused by the NATO bombing as well. Vlastimir Djordjevic had no knowledge of the fact that any crime of wanton destruction had been committed, and even if the Court ascertains that in certain cases there was intentional damage, Vlastimir Djordjevic was not in the field, in the area, and could not have seen anything like that taking place. As a summary of all this, the Prosecution attempted to insinuate the existence of some sort of plan on the basis of the crimes committed during a war, whereas there never was any such plan. In the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a state of war was proclaimed precisely at the moment when these unfortunate incidents took place. The fact that in war ugly things happen does not prove that an all-embracing plan existed for things like that to happen. The victims and fear were never part of any plan, but the results of these events. The Defence, in its final brief, pointed to ten other reasons for this population movement. See paragraph 729. In the absence of any proof and evidence of the existence of a plan, it is sufficient to look at a reasonable reason where we have reasonable doubt with respect to the existence of a tacit plan. We mentioned reasonable reasons for the movement of population; and, first of all, we'd like to focus on the non-selective bombing of NATO forces, the fear of people that they would be caught up in the cross-fire of combat, manipulation by the KLA, propaganda by the KLA and NATO. All these reasons throw great doubt on the reasons for which 800.000 people moved, for which Neil Wright says that to a large extent they were Kosovo Albanians, especially bearing in mind that a similar percentage of the non-Albanian population also left Kosovo. But this was recorded in a far less adequate way. Proof that a plan existed was compiled at top level and that Vlastimir Djordjevic knew about it is something that the Prosecution bases and sets out in paragraph 171 of its final brief. The allegations made in that paragraph are a drastic example of how the Prosecution makes its conclusions on the basis of incorrectly quoted witness statements and testimony, thereby manipulating the facts in order to prove their case. Paragraph 171 relates to a video recording of the rally of the Serbian Radical Party and Vojislav Seselj's speech at the rally. The video was compiled by the BBC and it was entitled: "The fall of Milosevic," and it was Exhibit P1510. We should like to ask you to focus your attention on that. Under quotations, the Prosecutor claims that Djordjevic's words, with respect to this video when they allegedly quote him and place quotation marks, they say that Djordjevic said as follows: "The parliament fully supported Milosevic's rejection of the conditions set out in Rambouillet as did the Serbian public. The Serbian deputy premier uncovered what Milosevic planned to do next. If NATO -- NATO starts bombing and if an American aggression takes place, we Serbs will suffer significant casualties, but there will be no more Albanians in Kosovo." And as a footnote, they mention the transcript of the testimony of Vlastimir Djordjevic, transcript page 10044 to 10045. The Defence was highly surprised and assumes that the Prosecution made a chance error in this particular case and not an intentional one, placing words into Vlastimir Djordjevic's mouth, something he didn't say, which is in complete contradiction with his response. All the words under quotation -- quoted under quotation marks as being uttered by Vlastimir Djordjevic were, in fact, the words of the BBC narrator from the video shown, and the transcript pages which the Prosecution quotes is from the audio recording of the video. Vlastimir Djordjevic's reply is to be found on the following page of the transcript, 10046, and it is completely contrary to what the Prosecution claims. This is what he said: "I really don't know anything about this rally of his, and otherwise it is well-known that he uses all -- every misfortunate that befalls the Serbian people for his own political gain, to score political points. He did not deliver this speech as the vice premier, and this is the first time that I see this. What he said over there, who was this binding upon? It is part of Seselj's political story. He always had some of his own comments to make, but all of them were to promote his own personal gain." Then on transcript page 10145 in response to the following question: "Did you not know that while you were planning the defence of the country, certain individuals in the leadership were bent on the expulsion of the population of Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo as a solution to the problem in Kosovo? Were you not aware of the fact that many people in the leadership expressed these same views?" And Vlastimir Djordjevic on that same transcript page replied: "Never did I hear anything like that from any politician, any such intent or any such plan or any such activity or anybody who was supposed to implement that plan if any kind of thing like that existed with respect to the expulsion from Kosovo and Metohija." This quotation I think best illustrates the Prosecution's designs by -- and in which way it quoted witnesses and drew conclusions and tried to prove mens rea with Vlastimir Djordjevic about the existence of a plan. Your Honours, I think this is the right time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. We will have the first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The Prosecutor did not prove how the Joint Command met in the course of 1999, or rather, how it might have co-ordinated the alleged expulsion plan. Joint anti-terrorist actions took place also in 1999; however, the so-called Joint Command, a task force which comprised a number of individuals and held regular meetings with Djordjevic in attendance, had been disbanded in 1998. Even if it had existed, Vlastimir Djordjevic could not be a member. Since paragraph 256 of the Prosecution brief alleges that the Joint Command comprised the senior MUP and VJ leadership in Kosovo and Metohija, the question arises as to how could Djordjevic be one of its members who often attended its meetings, bearing in mind that during the indictment period he was not in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, but rather in Belgrade. Vlastimir Djordjevic personally was unaware of the existence of any JC command which might have continued to work after the October Agreements. In terms of planning and implementation, the co-ordination of anti-terrorist activities involved the MUP staff of counter-terrorism and the Pristina Corps during the course of 1999 as well. There was never co-ordination at the MUP and Main Staff of the army of the 3rd Army level when it came to the planning or implementation of anti-terrorist actions. At the MUP level, no plans existed for active combat in the event of war. All MUP and RJB plans referred only to the preparation of their organisational units for activities in war time circumstances. Instructions provided by the RJB for preparations due to the threat of war were sent to all organisational units in the territory of Serbia which were duty-bound to act accordingly in the same way, both in Kosovo and Metohija and elsewhere. While the threat of NATO intervention was present in early January 1999, the General Staff of the Army issued the Directive Grom 3 and the 3rd Army an order for its units on the implementation of the General Staff directive. The Pristina Corps proceeded to elaborate the directive and initiated its order on 16 February 1999, and the main - and the MUP Staff, in view of the coordination achieved with the Pristina Corps command on 17 February 1999, at its own meeting at the Staff briefed the attendants about planned activities in case of NATO intervention. The record of that meeting shows that the briefing provided only general information and that further planning and elaboration was to be done with the commanders of the police units under the MUP Staff command. There is no evidence that Vlastimir Djordjevic or anybody from the RJB centre had participated in planning actions in Kosovo in case of NATO intervention. If such a plan had indeed existed at the RJB level, it would apply to the territory of entire Serbia because all RJB instructions uniformly regulated the actions of all organisational units in the territory of entire Serbia. The Prosecutor tried to demonstrate that Djordjevic on the 1st of June, 1999, went to the meeting of a Joint Command; however, there's no proof that he actually attended such a meeting or that in such a meeting was indeed a meeting of the Joint Command. With the only exception being Witness Vasiljevic's recollection that Djordjevic attended that meeting, but he didn't take the floor. However, he did not note Djordjevic's presence in his notebook and no other evidence of Djordjevic's presence at the meeting exist. Stojanovic testified and confirmed that none of the allegations are correct. Djordjevic himself stated that on that day he was not in Pristina and he did not attend any meetings. Witness Vasiljevic stated that he attended the meeting on the 1st of June, 1999, in Pristina together with Djordjevic and that the meeting had been presented to him as a Joint Command meeting. He did not consider himself a Joint Command member. Even if Djordjevic had possibly attended that meeting, that would not constitute proof that Djordjevic was a JC member in 1999. The OTP thinks that Vasiljevic doesn't have a motive to testify falsely and that Witness Stojanovic has such a motive. One has to bear in mind that Witness Vasiljevic provided his statements to the OTP as a suspect and that he had never received a notification that the OTP no longer treated him as such. Witness Stojanovic, on the other hand, was never a suspect. The OTP allegation in paragraph 1075 that Djordjevic as the highest-ranking MUP officer commanded and controlled MUP units and attached units during combat operations has not been proven beyond reasonable doubt. The OTP did not proffer evidence to corroborate such allegations. Article 54 of the regulation on the organisation of the MUP prescribes that departments are headed by chiefs of departments. This was corroborated by Djordjevic during his testimony when he explained the regulation on the internal organisation of the MUP, Exhibit P357. The notorious fact is that the regulation on the internal organisation of the MUP was passed by the minister of the interior and regulated the command of the MUP. However, the minister has the authority to change the MUP's competencies, organisation, and even responsibilities in keeping with the requirements and takes decision accordingly. With a view to provide for the most rational use of all MUP resources for anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija, the minister of the interior on the 16th of June, 1998, issued a decision on setting up a staff for countering terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija as an inter-departmental body. He outlined the Staff’s authorities and tasks as well as the responsibilities of the Head of Staff with regard to the Staff activities and the state of security with respect to the implementation of tasks that he was in charge of in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. By issuing this document, the minister derogated the authorities of both departmental chiefs onto the newly established staff and transferred their responsibility and authorities to the Chief of Staff. Sending RJB units to Kosovo and Metohija is part of the implementation of the decision of the minister of the interior. In the dispatches there is no reference to the task that those units were supposed to carry out. The deployed units received their tasks from the Staff, to which they reported about the activities that had been implemented. The police units in Kosovo and Metohija were answerable to and reported to the MUP staff about the tasks they had carried out and they are not answerable to the departments from which they had been sent. The regulation on the internal organisation of the MUP applies only to the organisation of the public security sector. The minister defined the organisation of the state security sector by a special regulation. Since these are two completely separate basic organisational units of the MUP whose only head is the minister, when issuing his decision on the establishment of the staff for countering terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, the Minister Stojiljkovic could not and indeed did not invoke the Rules on the internal organisation of the MUP, which applied to the RJB, Exhibit P357, or the Rules on the internal organisation of the RDB, Exhibit P1349. He found the legal foundation in Article 7 of the Law on Internal Affairs, Exhibit P66, and Articles 433, para 1, and Article 69 of the Law on State Administration, Exhibit P69. And thus derogated the provisions of the regulation on the internal organisation of the MUP and the regulation on the internal organisation of the RDB in the part providing for the responsibilities of both chiefs for the implementation of the tasks which he had transferred onto the MUP staff and established the responsibility of the staff for the implementation of the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrespective of their affiliation to the department --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will take care of that. Thank you. [Interpretation] Irrespective of their affiliation, all members of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija and all organisational units of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija were subordinated to the staff when it came to the implementation of the tasks of countering terrorism and special security tasks in Kosovo and Metohija, so that the number of members of one or the other department in Kosovo and Metohija who were involved in those tasks are not important. The MUP staff is a sui generis organ which was founded by the minister, and as such it acted exclusively on the minister's orders to whom it reported for the work within the scope of responsibilities that the minister entrusted to it. Witness Cvetic, the chief of the SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica, confirmed that the task of the staff in anti-terrorist activities and what those tasks were, but he was not familiar with the minister's decision on the establishment of the staff for countering terrorism, Exhibit P57, and the responsibilities of the Chief of Staff and his answerability to the minister and not to the chief of the RJB. His opinion about the nature and the role of the staff of the MUP in the organisation and management of the MUP are not important. And based on the evidence, the Trial Chamber will make inferences about this disputable issue. About its work and the work of the staff for countering terrorism as well as of all the planned and implemented actions in Kosovo and Metohija, the Chief of Staff reported to the minister. There is no single piece of evidence that he reported to the chief of the RJB about any of those issues. If Lukic went to Belgrade every week in order to report back to Stevanovic and Djordjevic and the Prosecution refers to Witness Byrnes in footnote 746 to prove that. However, the witness heard all that from Lukic. He does not have first-hand knowledge about all that. In the Milutinovic case he also mentioned that Lukic told him that Stevanovic was the one who was reporting, and in this case he also added Vlastimir Djordjevic to that. Byrnes provided quite a number of illogical facts in his testimony. For example, that Lukic took over the function of the Head of Staff from Stevanovic, who was his predecessor, and the evidence here has established that the Head of Staff, created at that time by the RJB Chief, was Aco Vesovic. Witness Byrnes had no knowledge about the structure and functioning of the MUP, as he, himself, confirmed. Therefore, he was not in a position to know who was reporting to whom about what and who was answerable to whom and for what. The way the MUP of the Republic of Serbia received information was regulated by an instruction which regulated the obligation of all organisational units about daily reporting in the territory of Serbia.
