Now, the fact that information of this kind does not and must not have any weight as proof or evidence in any court proceedings is something that all the witnesses said, policemen who know what an Official Note looks like and what form it must take and what information it must contain. Golubovic, Radojkovic, and even Witness K84 himself, claiming that they were only for local use, confirmed that the papers which were compiled by the Working Group and were titled Official Note, could not be used for any official purpose, least of all as a piece of evidence in court. And I refer you to Article 83 of the ZKP. Despite all the weaknesses with respect to what the witnesses said regarding the Official Note, K87 and K93 said that the statements contain large number of untruths and that 90 per cent was the free interpretation of Witness 84, whereas for certain serious accusations they termed them as lies and said that they had never uttered them. These two witnesses were precisely the witnesses who spoke about the bodies and the way in which Djordjevic acted with respect to the bodies in Serbia. And it is not by chance that these untruths are to be found precisely in their Official Notes. And referring in paragraph 1194 about Djordjevic's order for the -- to destroy the refrigerator truck found in Kladovo, the Prosecutor fails to mention that it was the minister's order which Djordjevic merely conveyed on to Golubovic. In paragraph 1195, a reference is made to the district prosecutor Krstimir Nestorovic who told the task force that the case was proclaimed a secret and that the general public should not have been informed about anything, and that was based on the hearsay testimony of Witness K84. The task force and Witness K84 were never interviewed by the aforementioned prosecutor, and there is no single piece of evidence that points to the case being in any way proclaimed a secret. When Prosecution witnesses were interviewed about this, the following is what is said about the matters. Witness Golubovic confirmed that the information on what had happened was never classified; on the contrary, statement of judicial bodies were not even warned not to talk about what they had seen. Classified information primarily referred to the state of war which had been proclaimed in the vicinity of the Romanian border and that was to prevent the onset of panic among the population and the traffic being interrupted on the main road. When it comes to the allegation in paragraph 1195 that the investigation was stopped and that the instruction came from the highest level in Belgrade, which at that moment were minister -- the minister and Djordjevic, we did not hear any testimony or see evidence to corroborate such allegations. Again, these are uncorroborated statements and unfounded conclusions, and not only that. The Prosecutor completely ignores K84's testimony and his answer to the question as to how come that during his two previous testimonies he failed to mention that Djordjevic had said to Prosecutor Nestorovic that all should be classified. He answered this: "Actually, those were rumours. Rumours had it that it all had come from the highest level. In the way I see it, why would Djordjevic call the prosecutor in Negotin? He would have called Golubovic. That would have been the chain of command, the appropriate chain of command, but those were rumours." In transcript page 2119. Thus, based on rumours, the Prosecutor in his final brief in paragraph 1195 draws its conclusion, failing to mention rumours about Djordjevic contacting Prosecutor Nestorovic in Negotin from the highest level in Belgrade and ordering him to keep everything a secret. Such an inference is inappropriate and malevolent. A huge injustice would be done to anybody who was convicted based on the evidence and interpretation of evidence of this kind and charges brought against the accused in this way. Witness Golubovic stated -- Witness Golubovic stated that the district judge and prosecutor were informed, they were informed by the municipal judge and the prosecutor who were at the site, and they were also informed to the duty -- through the duty service in Kladovo which informed the judge in Negotin. Witness Radojkovic stated that it was impossible for the police to force the judiciary to come to a crime scene. They could also not park the truck full of bodies by the road and wait for the judiciary bodies to turn up. An analysis of the evidence and the witness testimonies clearly demonstrate that the Prosecutor's conclusion in paragraph 1199 is not founded on the evidence presented during the trial and also that such a conclusion cannot be made beyond reasonable doubt. It cannot be claimed that Vlastimir Djordjevic, the minister, or anybody else for that matter, had no intention to perform post mortems in keeping with the procedure. Vlastimir Djordjevic did intend for the procedure to be followed at the moment when he learned from Caslav Golubovic about the existence of the bodies. At the moment when he learned about the existence of the bodies, he ordered a team to be set up to investigate the facts. At that moment, Vlastimir Djordjevic didn't know who the bodies belonged to, he didn't know who the people were who had lost their lives, he didn't know where they had lost their lives, how, he didn't know whether they had ever been buried, and he didn't know where they were being transported from and how and let alone who the transport was organised by. The investigating judge and the prosecutor of the municipal court came to the crime scene, together with a pathologist. When they left the crime scene, the district prosecutor and the investigating judge were informed about everything, both by the MUP, the duty service, as well as by their colleagues from the municipal court. The MUP could not force the judiciary bodies to come to the crime scene. At that moment, the aggression of the NATO forces and the shelling are under way. The state of war had been proclaimed. Everything was happening close to the Romanian border by a very busy road and the lorries by the road and an unbearable stench was coming from it. Something had to be done, even if the judiciary bodies had not come to the crime scene. Thus, they were informed, but they didn't turn up and there was no way for the MUP to force them to go to the crime scene. The story about the secrecy of the matter is based on the testimony of Witness K84 about rumours, whereas the eye-witnesses present an entirely different story. Clearly, the OTP's wrong when they allege that Djordjevic's only intent was to cover up the whole matter. The exact was opposite. Djordjevic did not do anything to cover up the facts about the refrigerator truck being found in Tekija. Just like the allegations in paragraph 1199 is not correct, one cannot accept the allegation that the actions to cover up the bodies in Batajnica continued for the next two months. It has been clearly demonstrated through the trial, which was corroborated by Witnesses K87, 88, and Djordjevic himself. The burials went on for no longer than 20 days. No single piece of evidence adduced during the trial points to the conclusion proffered by the Prosecution in paragraph 1200 when they claim that it was either Djordjevic himself on his own who organised the transport of the bodies from Tekija to Batajnica or in concert with the minister. This conclusion is based on assumptions and it certainly cannot be drawn beyond reasonable doubts as the evidence shows that somebody else from the ministry and not Djordjevic participated in the transport of the bodies, and that it was somebody else from the ministry, and not Djordjevic, who spoke to Golubovic and driver Ursuljanovic about the transport of those bodies. It can be clearly concluded that Witness K93 was sent to Tekija and later on to Batajnica by Assistant Minister Zekovic and not Djordjevic. This all tallies with the moment when Djordjevic said to the minister, "I no longer wish to participate in all this," and the moment when the minister said that, the transport of the bodies was his concern from then on. The same paragraph brings another conclusion, and that is that it is not realistic to believe that Djordjevic distanced himself from the whole matter at that moment, and that only a few days later he participated in the burial of the bodies in Batajnica. There is a very clear explanation for this erroneous conclusion on the part of the OTP. The OTP fails to state the fact that the minister called General Vlastimir Djordjevic to his office in April 1999, a few days after he received information from Perucac lake and told him that the trucks which transported the bodies from Tekija was then in the area where the special anti-terrorist unit had its own shooting range and that the bodies were supposed to be buried there. That was the 13th May centre in Batajnica. What ensued was a discussion involving General Djordjevic and the minister, and then the minister said to Djordjevic -- reminded him, rather, that the latter had already refused to carry out his direct orders on two occasions and that was with regard to Tekija and Perucica but the situation was very serious, that the war was going on, that the entire territory of Serbia is subject to major destruction, and that at that moment that was the way to deal with the bodies in Batajnica. General Vlastimir Djordjevic at that moment, bearing in mind the situation in Serbia, the shelling and destruction across the entire territory, he caved in and he accepted to carry out the minister's order. That is why seven to ten days later after the discovery of the refrigerator truck in Tekija, Vlastimir Djordjevic participated in the burial of the bodies in Batajnica. That was the moment when Vlastimir Djordjevic actually learned that the bodies from the refrigerator truck in Tekija were to be found in Batajnica, and that was the moment when Vlastimir Djordjevic learned about the true intentions of the minister. That was the moment when Vlastimir Djordjevic accepted to participate in the burial of the bodies in the area of the 13 May centre in Batajnica, not before, no way. The Prosecutor, in paragraph 1202, concludes that Djordjevic, in his defence, tried to pass on the entire responsibility onto the minister; however, that that was entirely unimportant with regard to the indictment, since together with the minister and some other key political, military, and police figures he's charged with having committed the crimes so that the participation of any other person does not deny his individual responsibility. This paragraph shows the essence of the erroneous and intentional interpretation of Djordjevic's defence and evidence presented during the case in order to support the Prosecutor's allegation. In paragraph 567 of the OTP, there is no reference or evidence with regard to the bodies which appeared in Perucac lake. In the second sentence it is stated that the bodies were collected and buried under Djordjevic's command. An entirely different situation can be found in paragraph 1203, where the OTP's trying to use the statement of Djordje Keric, who was at the time the chief of SUP in Uzice. He presented several contradictory statements in order to explain his own role and the role of Vlastimir Djordjevic in the whole chain of events. A further analysis will show that Witness Keric, in an entirely unconvincing way, tried to explain how come that under oath before the Trial Chamber of the district court in Belgrade he provided a statement which was totally contrary to the statement that he also under oath provided to -- before this Trial Chamber. In paragraphs 1203, 1204, and 1205, based on parts of the statement of Djordje Keric in different proceedings, the OTP again proffers half truths, and even those half truths are contradictory and are not – do not tally with the presented evidence. For example, in paragraph 1205, it is stated that Djordjevic had ordered Zoran Mitricevic, chief of crime police of the SUP in Uzice, to be sent to the crime scene, although even Witness Keric in all of his statements said that it was he who had sent Mr. Mitricevic there and that Djordjevic's order was to check what was actually going on there. After several similar constructs in paragraph 1208, the OTP accept that Witness Keric on the 8th of June, 2005, provided a statement under oath to a judge of the war crimes chamber, at the District Court in Belgrade, Judge Dilparic, Exhibit D316, and that in that statement, he stated that in the absence of other instructions, a decision had been made by Mitricevic to bury the bodies in the immediate vicinity of lake Perucac where they had been found. In this paragraph the Prosecution accept that the testimony of Witness Keric given before this Trial Chamber is legally completely irrelevant as it contradicts previous testimonies. If we remember the testimony of Djordje Keric, provided in July 2009, and his comport and conduct before the Trial Chamber, one could clearly conclude that he was not telling the truth and that he was not in a position to explain 22 the numerous contradictions that he was faced with during the cross-examination. Despite that, in the same paragraph, the decision on the burial of the clothes [as interpreted] in the vicinity of Perucac lake is thus -- is ascribed only to Mitricevic, which is contrary to the Exhibit D316 presented during the trial. And this is what the evidence shows. A few days after the events in Tekija and Kladovo, General Vlastimir Djordjevic received an invitation from the chief of the secretariat in Uzice, Djordje Keric, who had informed him that some bodies may have appeared on Perucac lake and that they were floating on the surface of the water. When he received that information, General Djordjevic was taken by surprise and he ordered the former to check the information and to come back to him. Keric did come back to him and told him that in addition to the bodies there is also part of the trailer which can be seen and that it also contains some bodies. Vlastimir Djordjevic received the information and conveyed the information to Minister -- to the minister. Keric did not issue any order or instruction [as interpreted]. When he conveyed the minister -- the information to the minister, he also shared his position with the minister. He said that his position is unchanged and he didn't wish to have anything to do with the whole matter. The minister didn't provide any comments and didn't issue him any tasks or instructions. A couple of days later, Keric again called General Djordjevic and informed him that he had buried the bodies near the dam, and this is all that Vlastimir Djordjevic knew about the bodies in Perucac lake. Djordje Keric confirmed in his statement that everything was exactly as General Vlastimir Djordjevic stated. Djordje Keric stated under oath on 8 June 2005 before the district court in Belgrade, the Trial Chamber for war crimes and investigative Judge Milan Dilparic which can be seen in Exhibit D316, in his statement, Witness Djordje Keric in six different places to the questions put to him by the investigative judge about the role of Vlastimir Djordjevic in the burial of the bodies by the lake stated the following: "For a while, Zoran Mitricevic and I talked about what to do and finally we decided that we would recover the bodies from the water and that we would bury them close to the Perucac dam. Zoran, himself, suggested that and I don't think that we had any other possibility at the time. The chief of the department did not provide us with any instructions. We did not have any other way to act. We decided to recover the bodies from the water and to burry them. We had consulted with Zoran, we asked him what to do. His suggestion was for the bodies to be recovered and buried. I agreed with that. We didn't have any other possibility. Your Honour, nothing else could be done at the time." Further on he says: "We didn't have any other solution that would have come to us from Belgrade. We ourselves decided what to do with the bodies. There were no suggestions on the part of the department chief with regard to the bodies. The only thing that happened was what the chief said what happened is really wrong, is really bad. I said that since there was no clear position taken by the department chief, the bodies should be recovered and interred until further notice, until the investigation is completed, until it can be determined who did it and what was actually done." When you compare statements that Witness Keric gave to the war crimes chamber in Belgrade and before this Tribunal, it is clear that this witness cannot be trusted and that everything he stated before the ICTY, which is completely contradictory to what he had said before the war crimes chamber in Belgrade, is untrue, to put it in simplest terms. Witness Keric obviously knowingly tried to play down his role in the whole event and to falsely accuse Vlastimir Djordjevic for his actions regarding the bodies found in the Perucac lake. The statement made by Vlastimir Djordjevic regarding the bodies found in the Perucac lake is consistent, life-like, convincing, and based on other evidence. The allegations that Djordjevic had instructed Keric not to inform the public prosecutor and the judge are inaccurate and are designed to play down Witness Keric's personal responsibility and show his intent to levy unfounded accusations against Djordjevic which he tried to do directly before this Tribunal in his testimony. Unlike Keric, the accused Djordjevic stated in his evidence clearly and unequivocally that he had never told Keric not to relay the information that had been given to him to the investigating judge and the prosecutor. Any comparisons between the situation with the truck found at Tekija and the bodies found in the Perucac lake is inappropriate and unfounded. Djordjevic's actions in his conversations with the Bor SUP chief Golubovic were completely different and occurred in completely different circumstances than those when he dealt with the Uzice SUP chief Keric. In order to analyse everything that is said in the Prosecution final brief in paragraphs 568 through 581, and the conclusions made regarding the events in the 13th May centre in Batajnica, in paragraphs 1217 through 1226, we will try to explain the facts as they have been presented in the course of the proceedings here. The facts say that the minister invited General Vlastimir Djordjevic to his office in April 1999 a few days after the information had come in regarding the Perucac lake and told him that the trucks used to transport the bodies from Tekija were now located in the training area of the special anti-terrorist unit and that the bodies should be buried there. This was the 13th of May centre in Batajnica. There was a discussion between General Djordjevic and the minister, and when minister told Djordjevic that he had twice refused to obey a direct order from him regarding Tekija and Perucac and that the situation now was quite serious. He warned him that there was a war going on, that there was a lot of destruction in the territory of the whole of Serbia, and that this was what needed to be done with the bodies in Batajnica. The order was to inform the people from the SAJ who were in charge of the training area to bury the body in their centre. He told him that he should relay to them that those were the bodies of the victims of NATO air-strikes and the terrorists and that after the war ended there would be an exhumation and regular procedure would be followed. General Djordjevic then contacted Witness K87, who in turn tasked Witness K88 with burying the bodies. The minister informed Djordjevic about each and every truck that arrived in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica, and Djordjevic would in turn relay the information to Witness K87. Djordjevic never knew the time and the point of departure of the trucks that arrived in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica. These facts have been determined based on the hearing of the immediate participants, direct participants, in the burial of the bodies, Witnesses K87 and K88 and the Witness K93 and General Vlastimir Djordjevic, himself. In paragraph 576, the OTP quotes the evidence of Witness K87 regarding the broken trailer. Yet, on that occasion the OTP fails to quote from the evidence of Witness K87 where he speaks about his conversation with General Djordjevic, where general told him to mark in some way the spot where the bodies were buried in order for an exhumation to be carried out when the time came for that. The trailer truck was left there to mark the spot where the bodies were buried. When the Prosecution speaks about the testimony of Witnesses K87 and K88 in paragraphs 571 and 572 and the conclusions about the role of Lipovac and Basanovic in paragraph 1223, the Prosecution fails to quote what Witness K87 said about the event described by K88. Lipovac's only role was to bring the fuel that was put into the trucks on several occasions. So two witnesses say completely different things about the same event. And Witness K87 says that Lipovac never had anything to do with this whole thing, apart from bringing fuel for the trucks. In paragraph 577, it is stated that Witness K88, upon his return from Kosovo, took part in a number of additional burials. The Defence is in the dark as to where the Prosecution has come across this claim. This is an arbitrary claim and it contradicts the evidence of Witness K88, who confirms in all his statements that he was present in the period of 20 days -- over the period of the 20 days when the trucks arrived in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica and that he had gone -- and that he went to Kosovo after that. [In English] I will take just a minute more. [Interpretation] When it comes to the number of trucks brought to Batajnica, the Prosecution states there were six of those, referring to the evidence of Witness K88, but neglects to mention that in his statement, Witness K87, and in his evidence, Witness Djordjevic, claimed that there were three or four. Witness K88 states that K87 told him about the arrival of each and every truck, so this is his source of information. In paragraph 1220, the Prosecution is trying to determine when the first truck came to Batajnica and concludes that this was on the 8th of April, 1999. On that day Vlastimir Djordjevic did not have any information to the effect that there were any trucks in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica, least of all that there were any bodies in those trucks. The minister informed Vlastimir Djordjevic about the existence of those trucks a few days after the events at the Perucac lake, so it was sometime between the 15th and the 20th of April, which is consistent with the evidence of Witness K87, that General Djordjevic contacted him about a month after the war started, sometime between mid- and late April. This is yet another piece of evidence that shows that General Djordjevic learned at that time that the trucks with the bodies were actually in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica. As soon as he learned about that, and as soon as he accepted the orders from minister -- from the minister, Djordjevic contacted K87. Had he known about the existence of the trucks with the bodies and had he organised the arrival of those trucks to the centre in Batajnica, as the Prosecution alleges, certainly those trucks would not have been standing there at the training area for days, as Witnesses K87 and 88 say in their evidence, but Djordjevic would have contacted them earlier. This evidence by those witnesses confirm the Djordjevic defence case, that the whole process of burying the bodies in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica took 20 days at the most and not two months, as the Prosecution claims in several places in its final brief. I think this would be an appropriate time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume just after 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Before we continue, I would first of all like to thank the interpreters for bearing with me and for following me at my rate of speed, but there are two minor mistakes in the transcript. I think they need to be corrected and then I would like to say for the record that at page 76, line 7, [In English] And instead of "dresses," it should be in the record, "bodies." [Interpretation] So instead of the word "dresses" there would be the word "bodies." At page 76, line 21, the interpretation is wrong because it says that Keric never issued orders and it should read that orders were never issued to Keric. So now I will continue. If one reads carefully not only what the witnesses spoke about, but what the OTP has written in its final brief in chapter 3(B), item 5 [as interpreted], it is quite clear that these are events that took place in the period from the beginning and until the 29th of April, 1999, at the latest. And this corresponds to the time-period in which the bodies were buried in the 13th of May centre in Batajnica and it also tallies with what witnesses K87, K88, K93 spoke in their evidence and what the accused Djordjevic himself said in his defence. Our next topic is Petrovo Selo. Vlastimir Djordjevic does not have any knowledge or information about the bodies buried in Petrovo Selo. In the course of the trial, no evidence has been adduced to establish any ties between Vlastimir Djordjevic and this event in any way. The allegation the OTP makes in paragraph 1185 and 1230 that in the same time-period MUP covered up the bodies in the SAJ base in Petrovo Selo and that this was part of the same operation is entirely arbitrary and is not based on any facts or evidence adduced in the course of this trial. There is not any piece of evidence adduced in the course of the trial that would establish any link between Vlastimir Djordjevic and the events in Petrovo Selo. The first untrue claim made here is that the base in Petrovo Selo was an SAJ base. That is simply not correct. In the course of the trial the evidence of the witnesses clearly show that this was a PJP base. In the course of the trial it was likewise determined who directly participated in the burial of the bodies in Petrovo Selo. Witness K93 testified about that and identified persons who issued the tasks to him and persons that he communicated with. Vlastimir Djordjevic is not among them, and he even went a step further to state clearly: "I never communicated with Vlastimir Djordjevic and I never received any orders from him." Witness K93 testified about the transportation of the bodies to Petrovo Selo, stating that he received all the instructions related to the departure for Kosovo and the transportation of the bodies directly from the assistant minister, General Zekovic, and that once he was in Kosovo and Metohija he spoke on the phone with General Sreten Lukic, who was the head of the staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. In paragraph 1233, the OTP starts a sentence with the following claim: "Djordjevic was also with Lukic, his direct subordinate, involved in certain talks regarding the cover-up with Witness K93." As regards the conversation in Lukic's office between K93 and Lukic, Djordjevic was there for just a few minutes of it. The proposal that K93 should go to Bujanovac was given by Lukic before Djordjevic ever entered the office. At the time Djordjevic was already retired, and he was not in a position to agree or disagree with the decision taken by General Sreten Lukic, who was the chief of the RJB at the time. In its final brief, OTP accepts the evidence of Witness K93, but when he speaks about the return of Witness K93 from Petrovo Selo, that's paragraph 592, they, the OTP, says in quotation marks "because they needed it." That's what they say, quote/unquote, because they needed it when the OTP speaks about the truck that was used to transport the bodies to Petrovo Selo. If you look at the evidence quoted as the source for this claim or quote, since there is -- there are quotation marks here, it is not clear which document was actually used as a source for this claim. Witness K93 never stated that in his evidence before this Chamber or in his statement. That's Exhibit 1065 at pages 3 through 4, as indicated in the footnote 1433 in the final brief. Paragraphs 599 and 1232 are quite unclear. In those paragraphs the OTP states that three persons were found in Petrovo Selo, they were identified as the Bytyqi brothers, and that they had been transferred from the prison in Prokuplje to Petrovo Selo on Djordjevic's orders. If those allegations are made because the Prosecution failed to adduce any evidence in the course of the trial to link Djordjevic with Petrovo Selo and the grave sites found there, the Defence sees it as a desperate move and would not stoop to comment. If this is the way to prove Djordjevic's involvement in the murder of the Bytyqi brothers, we would like to note that proceedings are under way in Serbia in this case and that some persons are accused and Djordjevic only appeared as a witness in that trial. The names of the Bytyqi brothers, or any incidents related to them, are not covered in the indictment against Djordjevic before the ICTY and their names, the names of the Bytyqi brothers, are not listed in any of the annexes to the indictment. Any insinuation on the part of the OTP that the link between Vlastimir Djordjevic and the grave in Petrovo Selo is based on the fact that the refrigerator truck was found in the Danube near Tekija was based on the fact that the refrigerator truck found in the Danube near Tekija was destroyed there is completely unfounded and is contrary to the evidence adduced in the course of the trial. Witness Golubovic confirmed that he had relayed to his subordinates the order that the truck should be destroyed and not the location where the truck should be destroyed. Witness Radojkovic confirmed that after receiving an order from Golubovic he decided to destroy the truck in Petrovo Selo. He chose the location. In paragraphs 1227 to 1229 the OTP attempts to prove that the burial of the bodies in Batajnica was part of a greater plan devised at a higher level and that Djordjevic was in charge of the operation to cover up the bodies. The OTP bases its whole construction on a statement made by Zivko Trajkovic, the former SAJ commander, who -- to whom Djordjevic said in 1999 something along the lines of: That is the decision taken by people who are much more important than you and I, so don't ask me too much about it. And this formulation something like -- when he said "something like," is not by chance because that's what Witness Trajkovic said, that's how he put it when he recounted what Djordjevic had told him 11 years ago. So Trajkovic himself is not quite sure that Djordjevic said this, but the OTP has taken this as being certain evidence of it being a plan devised at a much higher level. Djordjevic in his statement clearly explained that the words quoted by Trajkovic is not what he actually said to him, and that's quite all right because Trajkovic himself does not claim that he remembers the authentic words uttered by Djordjevic, the accused Djordjevic, said that somebody above him decided about that and that is true. And that was the then-minister of the interior Vlajko Stojiljkovic. During the proceedings and Prosecution case, not a shred of evidence was presented to back up the existence of any plan at a higher level. During the proceedings, not a shred of evidence was presented to speak about the holding of a meeting at which assignments or roles were assigned in order to carry out the burial of bodies all over Serbia. During the proceedings, not a shred of evidence was presented to back up the OTP's assertion that the plan to cover up the bodies, in addition to the minister and Djordjevic other leading political military and political personages took part. Vlastimir Djordjevic was in Kosovo and Metohija in the summer of 1998, and there were also operations underway at that time. But as to the bodies that are alleged to have been buried then beyond regular procedure – no, there was nothing of the sort going on, nor were any bodies transported anywhere. Vlastimir Djordjevic had no reason to assume that anything like that would 21 happen ten months later because we assure that unless you take part in something like that it is difficult to assume that anybody in his right mind would think of such an idea, let alone put such an idea into practice. There is no plan, there is no previously issued task, there was no information or knowledge about the existence of bodies, there was no reason to assume that any such idea existed. And the next step was to organise transport from Kosovo and Metohija to the territory of Serbia proper and the question is: What role did Vlastimir Djordjevic play in that. An answer to that question is quite a simple one and can be summarised in Vlastimir Djordjevic's own words. In his defence he said: "I didn't know whose bodies were located in the truck that was found. I didn't know who those people were who had lost their lives. I did not know where they had lost their lives and in what way. I did not know whether they were buried nor did I know where they were from or in what way they were transported, let alone who organised the transport." The Trial Chamber was told quite sincerely that his -- Djordjevic told the Trial Chamber sincerely when he received the knowledge. He described in detail what his role was in the so-called cover-up of the bodies on his part and what his relationship was towards this act and how long everything lasted. The obvious surprise that he experienced when he heard for the first time of the existence of any bodies in the territory of Tekija is something that Witness Golubovic spoke about when he was heard before this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber. When he heard of the existence of any bodies on the territory of Uzice he was surprised, and he said, "What happened is not good at all," and that is something that Witness Keric said. Perhaps the best proof of Djordjevic's position in relation to everything that was happening at the time is something that K87 said during his testimony. He said: "I felt that everything that was happening was happening against the will of General Vlastimir Djordjevic, and I gained the impression that he hoped that everything would come to an end, that it would all be over." And then he goes on to say: "The general was nervous and deep in thought. That's the impression I gained. He told me that there was an assignment which we had to carry out and that that was our duty. Then he told me what it was about. He said that those people had to be buried. He said that they were the victims of NATO bombing and that we shouldn't talk too much about it, but that we should wait until the end of the war to carry identity the identification of those people so that they could be buried properly and that it was important to mark the spot where they were buried so that everybody would know where this was done and how it was done. It is clear," he concludes, "that Vlastimir Djordjevic was taken by surprise when -- about information on bodies in Serbia coming from Kosovo and Metohija. And it is clear that he had no information, nor did he, in any way, participate in the transport of bodies from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija to the territory of Serbia proper. We can clearly deduce that he never took part in any meeting in which he discussed the cover-up of Kosovo Albanians." Furthermore, the Prosecutor has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Djordjevic, by deploying volunteer and paramilitary units, contributed significantly to implementing the joint criminal enterprise by allowing their deployment and attaching them to the MUP units in Kosovo and Metohija. Vlastimir Djordjevic did not have any knowledge and could not have sent other units except the RJB units to Kosovo and Metohija pursuant to the minister's decision. There is no proof in evidence whereby Vlastimir Djordjevic had knowledge that in Kosovo -- to Kosovo and Metohija paramilitary units were sent outside the RJB. In these proceedings it has been established that only one group of reservists was attached to the SAJ units during the war, whereas the Prosecution claims that it is -- which the Prosecution claims is a paramilitary unit. Without entering into the question of whether the Skorpion units were added and attached to the SAJ, we must first look whether a unit was formed to protect the oilfields in Slavonia and whether it was a paramilitary units during the time of its formation and existence. Prosecution Witnesses K92 Stoparic and Trajkovic confirmed that the government decision and the Ministry of Defence decision of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem that a unit was formed to protect the oilfields and the borders at the end of 1992, which was included into the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and placed under the command of the Army of Srpska Krajina in 1995. The unit was disbanded, it handed over its weapons and equipment to the Army of Yugoslavia and ceased to exist. Members of the unit which called itself the Skorpions, after being disbanded up until the 25th of March, 1999, were never rallied into any unit whatsoever and did not undertake any activities at all. The second question which can be posed is what the composition of the reservists was who were attached to the SAJ, or rather, were they former members of the disbanded unit which provide security for the oilfields in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Once again, on the basis of Prosecution witness testimony, we can just conclude that a small number of the reserve force that was accepted were members of the disbanded unit from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Most of the men taken into the reserve formation had nothing to do with this disbanded unit. The next question which begs an answer is: How can a paramilitary unit exist without any equipment and arms? And we consider that it is not contested that the equipment and weapons were given to the reservists only once they had become part of the reserve force. There was no knowledge about the crimes committed by the members of the reserve of the MUP who were former members of the unit to secure the oilfields carried out during the war on the territory of the former SFRY at the time they were engaged in 1999, and this was confirmed by Prosecution and Defence witnesses alike and this -- knowledge about this was gained many years later. As to the earlier -- the criminal past and the events of the crime in Podujevo and members of the reserve force of MUP attached to the SAJ, there was more talk in the closing brief of the Defence. Djordjevic cannot be held responsible for sending any volunteer or allegedly paramilitary units to Kosovo and Metohija which was outside the RJB. Djordjevic just simply carried out decisions taken by the minister to deploy men to RJB units. All other paramilitary units mentioned by the witnesses, if they were sent, were not sent to units of the RJB nor were they sent by Vlastimir Djordjevic nor did he have knowledge of any sending of paramilitary units to Kosovo and Metohija as he clearly stated in his testimony. Now, why the reserve force was engaged in the first place and attached to SAJ units was explained in the Defence final brief. By way of speculative conclusions, the Prosecution charges Djordjevic with approving the taking in and engagement of the reserve forces in Kosovo and Metohija, both for the first time and the second time. If that allegation by the Prosecution were correct, then Djordjevic, at the request of Trajkovic, would have taken the decision straight away and there would be no need to defer any decision taking. After much discussion, Djordjevic told Trajkovic that reception into the reserve force and their deployment had been permitted, and Trajkovic testified before this court and said that the decision to engage the reserve force was something that only the minister could have taken and the person that he authorised would put the minister's decision into practice. This was confirmed by a number of other witnesses as well, and we can conclude this by reading the law governing the internal affairs. At the time when the reserve force attached to the SAJ was taken in and engaged, Vlastimir Djordjevic had no knowledge about any crimes which the members of this reserve force had committed on the territory of the former SFRY. Vlastimir Djordjevic had no knowledge of the fact that any individual members of the reserve force were ever on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the disintegration of the SFRY. He had no knowledge that these persons were members of units in Croatia which were called the Skorpions, nor did the name Slobodan Medic mean anything to him at the time when persons from the reserve force were taken in and deployed. Vlastimir Djordjevic had no knowledge nor is there any proof of that, whereby the members of the reserve force, members of the SAJ, were ever a paramilitary unit. His only knowledge was that some of these individuals were known to the SAJ commander Trajkovic, and K92 from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and that there were people from Novi Sad, Sid, Ruma, and the surrounding parts. Zivko Trajkovic, the commander of the SAJ unit, found and selected people to make up the reserve force. As there is lack of evidence, the Prosecutor relies on a statement made by K92 on the 29th of June, 2005, which is not an exhibit in these proceedings and it is cited in reference 3168 of the OTP's final brief. In footnote 3228, at the end of paragraph 1178, the OTP once again quotes from document P1595, without saying that the document was not admitted but just MFI'd and then links it with Vasiljevic to whom this document was never shown. The Prosecution, in the absence of evidence, is using documents which were not admitted into evidence in this case and upon which there -- a decision cannot be based. Paragraph 231 where they say that notorious paramilitary groups in 1998 went to Kosovo and during the period of the indictment they quote Vasiljevic, who, apart from the Skorpions, has no knowledge whether any other groups went to Kosovo and Metohija and Stoparic who exclusively talks about the Skorpions as being a reserve force which was attached to the SAJ and everything -- all this referred to 1999 and not 1998. Furthermore, as to the quotation the paramilitary units replenished the MUP units, there's no reference about that in that same paragraph. Paragraph 203 presents more constructs about special operations units and its alleged satellite units. Footnote 447 and 448 to corroborate the allegations, the Prosecutor quotes Witness Stoparic. However, the witness did not speak about Kosovo and Metohija, but rather about Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. And his testimony was unrelated to the special operations unit's structure and the indictment period. In paragraph 234, footnotes 519, 520, and 522, the Prosecution refers to Stoparic's witness, but that does not refer to Kosovo and Metohija but rather to Slavonia and Djeletovci. Footnote 523 in reference to official RDB and IDs, the Prosecutor refers to Vasiljevic's assumptions. In footnote 521, with regard to the presence of Arkan's Tigers in Kosovo, the Prosecutor quotes Witness K82, who, on page T8457, says that he personally doesn't know whether they were ever in Kosovo and Metohija. In paragraph 236, in footnote 527, the Prosecutor quotes Cvetic in respect of bullet point 7 of the dispatch dated 18 February 1999, Exhibit P356; however, the Prosecutor fails to refer to the transcript page T6679, i.e., the witness's explanation of the police jargon term "to put under operative control." In footnote 529, paragraph 236, the Prosecutor misquotes Witness Vlajkovic who, quite contrary to what the Prosecution alleges, says on the cited pages of the transcript that he has no knowledge of the use of paramilitaries by the MUP. No person's criminal past cannot -- can be established based on any witness statements, regardless of that person's position or function, especially bearing in mind that the evidence in question is supported by official records which are accessible. More specifically, when talking about MUP reserve forces and their members attached to the special anti-terrorist unit in Kosovo in 1999 who were charged with and convicted for the Podujevo crime, the RS MUP records do not contain information about their criminal records in the territory of the Republic of Serbia up to the moment when they were engaged, and those were the only records available to the MUP. When it comes to persons who were born outside of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, the MUP could not obtain their criminal records from their country of birth. It could only be done via the Ministry of Justice for individuals against whom criminal proceedings had been instituted in Serbia. I will apologise to the Trial Chamber and I will ask for a little bit more time if that is granted, I will be able to finish very quickly. In paragraphs 1183 and 1184 there is a reference to establishing a link between the SAJ unit and the attached reserve forces and the alleged PJP crimes and ethnic cleansing of Albanian villages. This is a result of the Prosecutor’s erroneous conclusion and failure to include evidence on the alleged crimes by the SAJ and attached units of reserve forces, from the statement of the OTP Witness Stoparic. The only conclusion based on Witness Stoparic's evidence is that they participated in anti-terrorist activities and that they -- that he did not see any civilians anywhere nearby. This is on page 2875 of the transcript. In paragraph -- just a moment. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of the sentencing, which is something that Defence has to present its position. As the counsel for the defendant, it is -- has been clear from the very beginning that Defence pleads for acquittal for the aforementioned reasons. We have tried to present the briefest possible summary of the reasons why the Defence believes that that would be appropriate, although this closing brief could go on much longer if we were to deal with everything that we couldn't tackle in the closing brief. The procedure is such that the Defence, just like our learned friends from the Prosecution, always have to deal with the matters that they need to explain themselves. We've tried to do that at this time in order to be able to clarify as many facts as possible. Therefore, once again, I would like to repeat that the Defence believes that acquittal is an appropriate decision for the defendant Djordjevic. The Defence, with all due respect, claims that even if all the allegations presented by the OTP, the proposed range would not be adequate. And bearing in mind that the Prosecution has not proven its allegations, the sentence range is not appropriate and when analysing the presented evidence, the honourable Trial Chamber will see that the allegations were not proven by the Prosecution beyond any reasonable doubt, which is quite appropriate because Vlastimir Djordjevic is not guilty of any accounts. We would like to bring our final argument to the end, and we would like to thank you for having read our final brief, based on which we would propose for Mr. Djordjevic to be acquitted on all counts. We would like to thank to the entire technical staff of this Tribunal. We would like to thank the Chamber's staff, the Registry staff, and all of those who have supported us in these proceedings. We would like to thank our colleagues from the Prosecution for their fair conduct and co-operation that has been extraordinary and contributed to these proceedings. I will also like to correct something in the record. On page 72, line 25, where it should say -- just a moment, please. Bear with me. I will have to consult my legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the receipt of those persons and their engagement. That would be all, Your Honours. Once again, I would like to thank you for your patience and we apologise for having tried to say as much as possible, and that's why we have had a problem with the interpretation and the interpreters -- but means most and that's how we acted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. The Chamber would like to thank counsel, both for the Defence and the Prosecution, for the way in which the case has been conducted, their attention to timeliness which has enabled us to finish the case in a faster time than most would have anticipated, and which I think from the quality of the written submissions that we have received and now the oral submissions, makes it clear that attention has been able to be focused primarily on the important matters of fact and law. All of that the Chamber appreciates and it will assist us in the task that lies ahead. Given that the evidence and submissions have now concluded, the hearing will be formally closed. The Chamber must reserve its decision and give consideration to the evidence and the submissions it has received. That, of course, is no short or easy task. We must apply ourselves conscientiously to that. We will deliver our decision as soon as we are clear in our ultimate finding about the matters in dispute and have prepared our written decision. We will attend to that with the same conscientious attention and attention to time that we know has been displayed throughout the trial by all. So thank you in the courtroom for your support. We will mention later how much the contribution of those assisting the courtroom has been. We now, therefore, reserve our decision and will deliberate in due course. You will be informed of the date of when we are ready to deliver.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.
